text: Since all BitcoinCash transactions are broadcast publicly, you can monitor the network and build fun interpretations of the data, visually and with sound. Sites like this have been around for a while, but I'll bet this is the first microtonal one with ghosts. It has a meditative, ambient sort of atmosphere, with clock-like chimes that can occasionally blend together into a single deep, brilliant tone. The geeky microtonal details: Each output of a transaction sounds a chime. The fundamental pitch of the chime is determined by the amount of BCH in that output. On a logarithmic scale, the amounts are mapped to the harmonics of 30 Hz, starting at the second harmonic for dust amounts (546 sats), up to 2100 BCH where it maxes out at the 31st harmonic. (So each harmonic has a range of output sizes that could trigger it. It's not fully continuous with output amount.) A chime's overtones are also selected from harmonics of a 30 Hz fundamental. I simply pick the harmonics that are closest to the frequency ratios of the overtones of an ideal metal bar. That does mean that chimes with fundamentals tuned to lower harmonics of 30 Hz will deviate more from those "ideal" (inharmonic) ratios compared to higher ones (since lower harmonics are further apart in pitch, so you have less resolution), but that was fine with me and I like the end result. I find it very meditative, like you're chilling in the clock dimension. When enough outputs of different sizes are triggered at the same time, you start to hear that warbly, inner-ear harmonic series buzz and the phantom fundamental tone, 30 Hz. Whenever a block (as in "blockchain") arrives, a bright timbre with harmonic overtones is sounded at 30 Hz, unifying the soundscape, if you will. There are lots of visual representations of the transaction data too. Each transaction is represented by a spirit whose size is determined by the transaction's size (in bytes, not amount sent). Their lantern color is determined by fee-rate (satoshis/byte), and each output is represented by a suitcase. Features like fungible tokens, NFTs, and OP_RETURN usage are indicated with various accessories. This was a fun opportunity to combine two things I'm extremely geeky about. I put it together for a Hackathon, but I'm sure I'll keep improving it. Thanks for reading!

text: > I've stopped trusting any of these influencer-benchmaxxers The influencer competition for attention in the LLM space is wild. LLMs have emerged as the topic of 2026, so all of the influencers who were previously scattered around topics like web dev, backend dev, product management, cryptocurrency, and every other niche have all pivoted into the same LLM influencer space. It’s like one big cage match where they’re all becoming increasingly cutthroat to fight for the dwindling scraps of attention in a crowded space. For the first half of this year it was interesting to see most of them move in unison on the hot topic of the moment, competing to have the best guides, hottest takes, and best courses (which are always shockingly expensive and no better than free content, but they encourage everyone to get their employers to pay). It was fascinating to watch them jump from topic to topic together, like when OpenClaw took off and they all had guides on personal agents or even created their own competing OpenClaw project. Or when MCP was the topic and everyone had the Ultimate Guide to MCP. Then some time this year everyone realized the space was too crowded and switch to contrarian hot takes: Every new model release had influencers making videos about how it was terrible, awful, and shouldn’t have been released. All of the old buzzwords got new videos like MCP IS DEAD with influencers going in the opposite direction of what they said 6 months ago. And now, the interpersonal drama is taking over. People like Theo are posting attacks and threats on others or bragging about blocking or getting blocked, which is the absolute last thing I want to read from supposed experts on a topic. Most sane people opt out of the influencer content after they realize how much it’s clickbait over quality, but all of these people also have rabid fan bases of people who can’t get enough drama and contrarian hot takes. It can be hard to filter out the contrarian hot takes when they get dressed up as new benchmarks or supposed revelations (declaring a model has been nerfed is evergreen) and cross posted to other sites.

text: $ETH.X Most self-proclaimed traders build their entire strategy around lagging indicators, mistakenly treating historical price data as a crystal ball for future market movements. Tools like moving averages, MACD, and RSI are mathematically designed to confirm trends that have already begun, not predict where price is heading next. By the time a golden cross appears or an oscillator signals overbought conditions, institutional algorithms and smart money have already captured the bulk of the move and are preparing to exit. Relying exclusively on these rearview-mirror metrics forces retail traders into a perpetual cycle of chasing momentum; buying near the top of a rally and selling at the bot

text: JPMorgan Puts Bitcoin Production Cost at $86,000 a Coin JPMorgan has lifted its estimate of what it costs to produce a single bitcoin to roughly $86,000, while the coin itself trades tens of thousands of dollars below that level. The figure comes from a bank report dated November 18, led by analyst Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou. It has climbed steadily through the year: $77,000 to $78,000 in June, about $85,000 by September. The market moved the other way. Bitcoin sat near $65,000 when the report was published and slipped below $60,000 two days later, widening the shortfall on every coin mined to more than $26,000. JPMorgan is careful with the number. It calls production cost a "soft floor" rather than a hard support level, because miners do not simply stop the moment a coin is worth less than its average cost of extraction. What the bank expects instead is adjustment: higher-cost miners selling part of their reserves to fund operations; some operators redirecting power and hardware toward AI infrastructure; weaker miners shutting down, which lowers hashrate and eventually pulls difficulty, and average cost, down. That last mechanism carries the argument. A sustained decline in hashrate would be evidence of capitulation, and JPMorgan's framework treats it as the path to cost relief even without a price recovery. The report also links the recent weakness to retail outflows from bitcoin and ether exchange-traded funds, together with shifting expectations around interest rate cuts. There is a feedback risk in the short term. Miners that sell reserves to stay afloat add supply to a market that is already short of demand. For anyone following the network, three signals matter from here: hashrate, difficulty adjustments, and ETF flows. 📷 Marko Ahtisaari · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons 🔗 Source: Crypto Briefing # Bitcoin # Crypto # Lightning

text: The # blockchain # tech itself is immaterial. The details don't matter. One could implement a "digital currency" and keep track of its transactions in some other way, but no matter the implementation it's still wholly dependent upon the illusion of virtuality, the false notion that the world of computing is somehow independent of the compulsory nature of corporations backed by governments. But let's assume for the sake of argument that it was somehow possible to implement such a system in an independent way. The easiest way would be to dispose of computers altogether and thus dispense of the extreme complexity of manufacturing them and maintaining them and interconnecting them, and implement an independent currency through physical means. Such a system could work: one could invent a totally independent currency that held good only within the limited scope of those people willing to honor the new currency's value. But this is NOT how # cryptocurrency is intended to work; it's certainly not how crypto is marketed. The dipshit Alyx ran into was spouting (on their blog) the typical crypto sales pitch--selling their blockchain trash by hyping it up as a good investment that was likely to increase in value, contrasting against evil Uncle Sam fiat petrodollars. But what is an # investment in the first place? It's something that's intended to be cashed out--in terms of hard currency, i.e. evil Uncle Sam fiat petrodollars. Without that possibility of converting crypto to real money, the techbro interest in the stuff would be practically nil.

text: $BTC.X The only way to confirm that the bottom is behind us is to look back in hindsight. This is the part of the cycle when most people have capitulated. You start seeing posts calling crypto a scam, with people predicting a recession or even a depression, especially in light of the historical stock market correction in Q4 of midterm election years. text: Malicious Ad Campaign Used iPhone Exploits to Hunt Wallet Seed Phrases A malvertising operation spent roughly six months turning ordinary online ads into a delivery system for iOS exploits, and crypto wallets were the prize. Confiant researchers, who call the campaign MoldyRoost, published their findings on Nov 20. The operation ran from May 12 to Nov 17, 2026 and was tied to more than 480 ad domains split across six clusters of activity. One cluster did most of the work: 403 domains, aimed mainly at Hong Kong, Japan and Singapore. The wider reach covered iPhones in 47 countries. What makes it uncomfortable is how little the victim had to do: A single tap on a programmatic ad opened a landing page built by the operators. That page delivered its code as it loaded — no download, no prompt, no second tap. Once inside, the implant searched Notes, messages, saved images and keychain data for wallet recovery phrases. The toolkit was aimed at iOS 13 through 17.2.1: 23 exploits arranged into five chains. Six further vulnerabilities targeted iOS 18.4 to 18.7, and three of them were zero-days at the time they were used. Confiant groups the exploit families under names such as Coruna and DarkSword; together the set covers 29 vulnerabilities across the older iOS releases. The implant looked for seed phrases belonging to MetaMask, Phantom and Trust Wallet — not because those apps were broken, but because of what people keep around them. A QR code sitting in a screenshot was as useful to the attackers as a note file. That is the detail worth sitting with. The weakness lived in Apple's operating system, not in the wallets. The practical response is unglamorous. Fully updated iPhones appear to be outside this campaign's reach, which puts patching ahead of any app-level fix. Seed phrases do not belong in Notes, in chat threads or in a camera roll. MoldyRoost is less a crypto story than a reminder of where the attack surface actually sits: the page you landed on for two seconds, and the file you saved two years ago. 📷 Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons 🔗 Source: Crypto Briefing # Crypto # Blockchain # Bitcoin

text: I think you missed the point of the comment. Yes, it's set up to be a market. But unlike say the stock market, where people try to do price discovery through analysis, prediction markets have been shown to have a vast majority of losers, and very few winners. It's more like a casino than a market, in its result. Though the house is this case is distributed. And really, the point from the parent comment that it's a way to monetize non-financial insider information is way more true than it's not. Prediction markets have turned out to not surface "predictions" so much as incentivizing people who factually know, to gain. The stock market lets me monetize a good guess, or my predictive research. "Prediction" markets are not about predictions. Unlike regular markets. Insider information on financials is way more controlled, too. If I had access to the next earning report and I trade on it, that's not really a "prediction", is it? Prediction markets are more like how bitcoin proves that nobody has a full quantum computer yet. It would just be too tempting to use it to steal bitcoins, as a converging instrumental goal.

text: Mining is one. This tweet is misleading, cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin are designed to work this way - the difficult of mining a coin automatically adjusts to be slightly less costly than buying a coin, giving miners a slim profit margin. Whenever the price drops some of those miners will no longer be profitable and they'll stop mining until the difficulty adjusts again or the price goes back up. Other network validation activities that can earn a return are staking, running masternodes for specialized networks (providing services or participating in governance), or operating mining pools. You can rent out storage capacity on decentralized storage networks or rent out spare CPU/GPU resources for distributed computing, provide services like blockchain data availability, or run other infrastructure such as indexes or RPC endpoints. Some protocols provide compensation for governance participation. You can lend it to borrowers to collect interest, provide liquidity for DeFi to get a share of trading fees, or provide liquidity to stabletokens to get return from trading fees or protocol incentives. A lot of this is very complicated, though, so people tend not to pay as much attention to it. "Buy low sell high" is easy to understand.

text: I mean, the article you posted doesn't address everything in my previous post. I'm still waiting for more info before conceding anything about how useful LLMs are in mathematical proofs specifically. As for the wider question about whether LLMs are "powerful" (whatever that's supposed to mean exactly)... I'm sure you must remember some of the ridiculous claims that were made about how Blockchain was going to change the world. Not only was it going to revolutionize how you payed for your groceries, but your house title would be on the blockchain, you'd use NFTs to get into venues, you could own NFTs for pieces of the Mona Lisa, Zuck's "The Metaverse(tm)" where you'd work your day job in the future, you'd vote in governmental elections using a blockchain and your wallet private key, you'd have your recovery passphrase stamped in solid metal buried in your back yard, and your biometrics data had to be on the blockchain for some dumbass reason. And all these revolutions were perpetually just a little ways off in the future. "Web3" they called it. At this point, most people look back on anything blockchain-related with embarrassment. The last time blockchain made the news was the last time someone in the Trump family ran another blockchain-related scam. Nobody has buttonholed me to tell me I should be mining Ethereum or whatever in quite a while. And nobody has asked in my employer's IT department all-hands meeting when the company is going to offer customers the option to pay with Bitcoin in a long time. The price of Bitcoin is still relatively high surprisingly and Tether hasn't collapsed to zero or anything yet, but the pool of people who still put any stock whatsoever in anything blockchain related is increasingly confined to weird little echo chambers that nobody else takes seriously. And it's clear at this point that blockchain is never going to be anything but a cringe gambling platform. (Let me pause at this point to say if you're still emotionally invested in anything blockchain-related, we might as well end this conversation here because it's clear there's no hope for ever reaching any consensus.) And guess who brought you the AI bubble. Sam Altman was the one behind [Worldcoin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_(blockchain)), that biometrics-on-the-blockchain thing I mentioned in the previous paragraph. CoreWeave was a cryptocurrency-mining company. Elon Musk. Donald Trump. When the snakeoil salesman gets outed as a fraud and then comes back a decade later with an ostrich oil concoction (that *definitely* isn't just overpriced mineral oil) that'll cure your sleep apnea 100% for sure this time I swear, the proper response is a whole lot of skepticism. And they're making the same kind of outlandish claims about AI as they did about blockchain. 10x/100x. Photoshop clones. Train an AI to act like you so your family can keep talking to you after you die. You can let the agent make restaurant reservations for you, no supervision needed; the restaurant won't even be able to tell it's an agent. Videos of 6-monitor computers running futuristic-looking "dashboards" overviewing the extremely profitable enterprise that "Jarvis" supposedly created/maintains autonomously for the video's creator. Remember that thing where they were going to recreate Minecraft and Doom except every frame was just Stable Diffusion output and there was no persistent game world or engine behind it beyond the user's key presses being fed to the image generator somehow? What did they call that, "vibegaming" or something? Not to mention TESCREAL or trying to convince religious leaders that Claude is conscious or AI doomerism claims like "X% chance it'll extinct humanity". Meanwhile, as I mentioned in my previous post, aside from *maybe* the mathematical proofs, there's currently no reason to think anyone's ever gotten any benefit out of an LLM beyond anecdotes. And enough of those are clearly delusional that it's worth scrutinizing the maybe-less-unhinged-sounding ones. That's largely why these claims about mathematical proofs seem so suspicious to me. Software development teams using LLMs are *less* productive and have more outages. Everything in entertainment with even a faint whiff of slop elicits only hatred from normies. OpenAI, Anthropic, even Google are losing *ridiculous* amounts of money on LLMs with no sign of profitability in sight. They're having to subsidize their own users to get anyone to use products like ChatGPT and Claude. Local LLMs aren't much cheaper if at all. Even if LLMs *were* useful, they'd be prohibitively expensive if they weren't subsidized. And yet, after a million different claims about LLMs being useful turned out to be hogwash, I'm supposed to believe this one? Of course, I will when there's sufficient evidence, but I've seen similar claims turn out to be laughably and obviously false to take this one with a salt lick. So, I hope that all makes it clear why I'm skeptical of the mathematical proof claims. And any other claims that LLMs are "useful". But back to your core question. "What would it take for your to believe that LLMs are actually incredibly powerful?" Again, it really depends what you mean by "powerful". I mean, if they could do things reliably without a human there to correct them (without ending up in the national news, that is) or if it could be demonstrated that it could make people actually more productive without making them stupid or the product inferior or if it could enable people to do worthwhile things that nobody could do before *and* if it could do at least one of those things at a cost that wasn't prohibitive (without being subsidized), then I'd admit it was at least to some extent "useful". The whole "making people stupid" thing in particular makes me extremely reticent to *ever* voluntarily touch an LLMs with a 10ft pole even if I believed them to be useful. Not saying I'd keep refusing to do so if my boss made my paycheck contingent on using them. I'm lucky not to be in that position. But I've built a career on my smarts. And nothing I've seen about LLMs leads me to think I won't need those smarts in the future. Quite the opposite. Fixing the slop (as Cory Doctorow calls it, "the digital asbestos we're shoveling into our walls") after bosses figure out it needs fixed is going to require a lot of problem-solving skill. And the ones who haven't succumbed to LLM-induced learned helplessness are going to be more effective at that than the ones who have. Plus, the kind of fun I like to have outside of work is the kind of fun that requires flexing my brain a lot. If I surrendered my brain to the LLMs, I'd lose basically *the* part of myself that I most value. And not just because it's the part I can wield to get a paycheck by delivering value to shareholders. Because it's a big part of what makes me me. It's core to my identity, and necessary to the things that give me joy. Aside from all that, I find LLMs unethical and would avoid using them on that basis. They give people I've never met asthma, contribute to global warming, consume shit-tons of water, and destroy ecosystems for huge data centers.

text: I was shooting heroin and reading “The Fountainhead” in the front seat of my privately owned police cruiser when a call came in. I put a quarter in the radio to activate it. It was the chief. “Bad news, detective. We got a situation.” “What? Is the mayor trying to ban trans fats again?” “Worse. Somebody just stole four hundred and forty-seven million dollars’ worth of bitcoins.” The heroin needle practically fell out of my arm. “What kind of monster would do something like that? Bitcoins are the ultimate currency: virtual, anonymous, stateless. They represent true economic freedom, not subject to arbitrary manipulation by any government. Do we have any leads?” “Not yet. But mark my words: we’re going to figure out who did this and we’re going to take them down … provided someone pays us a fair market rate to do so.” “Easy, chief,” I said. “Any rate the market offers is, by definition, fair.” He laughed. “That’s why you’re the best I got, Lisowski. Now you get out there and find those bitcoins.” “Don’t worry,” I said. “I’m on it.” I put a quarter in the siren. Ten minutes later, I was on the scene. It was a normal office building, strangled on all sides by public sidewalks. I hopped over them and went inside. “Home Depot™ Presents the Police!®” I said, flashing my badge and my gun and a small picture of Ron Paul. “Nobody move unless you want to!” They didn’t. “Now, which one of you punks is going to pay me to investigate this crime?” No one spoke up. “Come on,” I said. “Don’t you all understand that the protection of private property is the foundation of all personal liberty?” It didn’t seem like they did. “Seriously, guys. Without a strong economic motivator, I’m just going to stand here and not solve this case. Cash is fine, but I prefer being paid in gold bullion or autographed Penn Jillette posters.” Nothing. These people were stonewalling me. It almost seemed like they didn’t care that a fortune in computer money invented to buy drugs was missing. I figured I could wait them out. I lit several cigarettes indoors. A pregnant lady coughed, and I told her that secondhand smoke is a myth. Just then, a man in glasses made a break for it. “Subway™ Eat Fresh and Freeze, Scumbag!®” I yelled. Too late. He was already out the front door. I went after him. “Stop right there!” I yelled as I ran. He was faster than me because I always try to avoid stepping on public sidewalks. Our country needs a private-sidewalk voucher system, but, thanks to the incestuous interplay between our corrupt federal government and the public-sidewalk lobby, it will never happen. I was losing him. “Listen, I’ll pay you to stop!” I yelled. “What would you consider an appropriate price point for stopping? I’ll offer you a thirteenth of an ounce of gold and a gently worn ‘Bob Barr ‘08’ extra-large long-sleeved men’s T-shirt!” He turned. In his hand was a revolver that the Constitution said he had every right to own. He fired at me and missed. I pulled my own gun, put a quarter in it, and fired back. The bullet lodged in a U.S.P.S. mailbox less than a foot from his head. I shot the mailbox again, on purpose. “All right, all right!” the man yelled, throwing down his weapon. “I give up, cop! I confess: I took the bitcoins.” “Why’d you do it?” I asked, as I slapped a pair of Oikos™ Greek Yogurt Presents Handcuffs® on the guy. “Because I was afraid.” “Afraid?” “Afraid of an economic future free from the pernicious meddling of central bankers,” he said. “I’m a central banker.” I wanted to coldcock the guy. Years ago, a central banker killed my partner. Instead, I shook my head. “Let this be a message to all your central-banker friends out on the street,” I said. “No matter how many bitcoins you steal, you’ll never take away the dream of an open society based on the principles of personal and economic freedom.” He nodded, because he knew I was right. Then he swiped his credit card to pay me.

text: > That changed as things like pensions and longevity awards went away thanks to MBAs MBAs and their groupthink are one thing and bad enough, but IMHO the true danger comes from what replaced pensions - the stonk market - that created that groupthink. Basically, before 401ks and other retail investment vehicles appeared, the stock market's primary function was to collect money from large scale investors (banks, insurances and the likes) and put it to productive usage. Boring stuff. But once people's retirements were tied to the stock markets, the stock markets were societally and thus politically forced/incentivized to always go up, and that meant that there suddenly was a large, continuous influx of capital to nowadays the tune of dozens of billions of dollars a month. That in turn meant a huge incentive to siphon tiny margins off of all the trades (which led to HFT being a thing) and a constant incentive for C-level leadership to engage in all kinds of shady deals to appear better to the markets - complex webs of shell companies to avoid taxes, financial fraud, sale-lease-back vulturism destroying entire companies... And it turned out, there was so much money flowing into the US retirement savings system that it couldn't be soaked up by the American economy alone, which led to American companies and investment vehicles buying up assets across the world, treating them just the same - and the work we do outside the US is slaving away for some American boomers' retirement. The result of that was eventually the 2007ff financial crisis, where dumbass investments by a single bank was enough to trigger the entire world economy to crash, then we had dumbass money hype up cryptocurrencies, and now we have dumbass money blowing up the AI bubble - which probably will explode much, much harder than 2007ff. text: > You might want to read a bit about Bitcoin scarcity, how it stays scarce and how its scarcity compares to other things. Just being scarce isn't enough though. It has to have fairly universal desire to be owned, meaning people must attribute value to it. There were a limited run of trading cards produced for the 1980s TV show ALF making them pretty scarce, but I think you'll be hard pressed to find someone willing to take ALF cards over gold as a unit of trade. Gold, for better or worse, has a long historical acceptance as a transportable unit of wealth across nations, cultures, and governments. No one needs to be convinced that gold has value, or that it will still have value 50 years from now. So the real question for Bitcoin is: Are the majority of people that hold it truly valuing it as a substitute for a unit of transportable wealth or are they engaged in gambling hoping for *greater fool theory*? I'm sure the answer is "its a mix of both", but it certainly looks like its far fewer true believers and far more get-rich-quick chasers.

text: There's no "design" here. Individual participants make their own investment decisions on building out the servers to mine Bitcoin at scale, and then over the useful life of that hardware it mines Bitcoin when profitable and then the hardware is retired or sold for another purpose once it's no longer profitable. They plan things out with an assumption about energy costs, Bitcoin prices, etc., and sometimes those long term projections turn out to be wrong to where they have to retire the hardware earlier than initially planned, or having a lower utilization rate over the course of its useful life, and they lose money on that. The macro equilibriums make the system as a whole survive, but individual players can and do get wiped out from shifts in prices that break their assumptions. And sometimes it swings the other way, too, where they make windfall profits they weren't expecting.

text: I was doing my security review last month and my biggest worry was a compromise in Bitwarden, but the issue was more the a bad extension gets pushed than the actual database being dumped out. I decided it was the same risk with Vaultwarden but with more stress on me having to actually maintain it. I'm not sure there really is a good hosted solution that removes that risk. I disabled auto-updating on my extension so at least hopefully I'm running a non-pwned version but at some point you have to update and there is no "lag-time" setting for extensions. I did use KeePassXC years ago but the sync there was always a pain, and you're just back at the "trust random app-store/fdroid developer is a good actor/not compromised" problem and it's probably easier to target one random guy (which might just be, here's a stack of bitcoin, leave your front gate unlocked on the 17th) than a big company who's whole job is password management. Whole thing sucks tbh.

text: Except this is actually how it was meant to work all along. Really, this *is* the design. Miners are supposed to join or drop from the blockchain based on whatever economic incentives make sense to them, it's not the blockchain's responsibility or role to "manage" them in any other way. If a miner has come up with some kind of special deal for electricity or is accounting for depreciation in some idiosyncratic way, that's fine - that's on them to handle. The Bitcoin blockchain doesn't care about that, it's designed not to *need* to care about that. All it cares about is the rate at which blocks are being found, not who's finding them. That's the only "feedback" mechanism built into Bitcoin. If blocks start coming in too fast the difficulty rises at the next adjustment period. If they're coming in too slow the difficulty falls instead. The underlying reasons for those changes are simply not relevant. Could be legal issues, could be electricity market forces, could be new types of mining hardware being invented, doesn't matter.

text: And I'm describing how that mechanism *doesn't actually push the cost of mining below the cost of buying an existing Bitcoin*. Bitcoin miners are continuing to mine at a loss, which is keeping the difficulty higher than the average miner's costs. In other words, mining isn't guaranteed to be profitable either for any given individual miner or for miners on average, and there is no design that ensures that it does. To whatever extent there was intention behind the design, it either isn't directed at miner profits at all, or has failed in its design to keep miner profits near zero. That's what I've been saying this whole time. There is no design for the profits or losses to play out in any particular way.

text: Ethereum is preparing for one of the most consequential security transitions in its history—and artificial intelligence, not just quantum computing, is driving the urgency.In a newly published technical recommendation, the Ethereum Foundation selected Keccak-256 as its foundational hash function to counter both quantum computing risks and AI-assisted cryptographic attacks. The decision followed an evaluation of five candidates: Keccak-256, SHA-256, Poseidon, BLAKE2, and BLAKE3. While newer alternatives like BLAKE3 and Poseidon offered speed advantages, the Foundation ruled them out due to limited attack-resistance research or vulnerabilities in reduced-round configurations. Meanwhile, advances in zero-knowledge proving infrastructure—such as Ethereum's leanVM—have narrowed the performance gap, allowing developers to prioritize Keccak-256's nearly two-decade security track record. Because Keccak-256 is already integrated into Ethereum's execution layer for address generation, client teams can reuse existing software rather than introducing new complexity. According to Ethlabs co-founder Julian Ma, while post-quantum readiness remains a core goal targeted for December 2029, AI represents an immediate threat capable of probing cryptographic weaknesses today. The Foundation has also doubled its protocol security team to accelerate formal verification ahead of a roadmap review in January 2027. For institutional investors and builders alike, the message is clear: as AI reshapes cybersecurity, longevity and mathematical certainty are becoming blockchain's most valuable assets. # Ethereum # Cybersecurity # QuantumComputing # ArtificialIntelligence # Blockchain

text: Leaked documents reveal the Russian anti-sanctions machine’s internal playbook for Chinese banks, including planned payment routes. Leaked files from inside Russian payment giant A7 shed new light on the methods the network uses to trick international banks into processing billions of dollars worth of transactions in evasion of Western sanctions. The cache of documents illustrates the depth of knowledge that personnel at A7, which the US Treasury designated as a “transnational criminal organisation” last month, possess regarding compliance triggers for suspect payments routed to China. The leak covers internal planning documents from A7 up to September 2026, and has not been previously reported. ... The new data underscores **A7’s strategic focus on China**, following the gradual tightening of sanctions over the last year as Western governments became aware of the sophistication and range of A7, spanning cryptocurrency, traditional banking, capital markets and trade finance. The files, some as recent as September 2026, suggest that Russia’s access to the Chinese economy is faced with barriers stemming from Beijing’s desire to insulate itself from the risk of US secondary sanctions, while the A7 organisation appears to operate with impunity despite the barrage of Western penalties against it and its owners. **Chinese banks are the primary destination for the Russian clients** of A7, which aims to secure frictionless payments Russia’s trading partners. ... The major channel for the first-leg transfer of A7 client funds into foreign banks and out of PSB, a sanctioned Russian state bank which is also A7’s co-owner, has been Kyrgyzstan, according to previous A7 leaks in late 2025. Deploying a network of shell companies with accounts at major banks, A7 uses an AI tool to generate fake invoices and other paperwork to support transactions outside of Russia that are, in fact, for Russian companies, according to the Open Source Centre, a UK non-profit that has investigated A7. ... But what the new documents reveal is how closely A7 personnel watch compliance procedures at Chinese banks, and their own internal guidance on how to avoid tripping them when sending payments on behalf of Russian importers. “Avoid these inspection triggers: avoid new suppliers (less than 6 months of operation), don’t use sensitive HS codes [standardised customs codes for specific kinds of goods] unless you need to, avoid round amounts,” one internal presentation on Chinese banks, dated August 2026, recommends. ... For payments related to “sensitive goods”, it recommends staff “prepare an export license” from China’s Ministry of Commerce, “check the goods do not appear in lists of dual-use goods”, and “prepare a certificate for the end use” of the items. The same document contains notes on “important thresholds” for payments, including a 200,000 yuan trigger for an automatic inspection by bank compliance. ... The leaked presentation also contained instructions for “difficult” banks, including recommendations on how to write customs codes and the exact number of characters a user can input into specific fields – to avoid a payment being refused. “China’s first priority is to protect its financial system, and to ensure that payments are properly documented,” says Chigadaev. “The second priority is commercial. **Chinese banks and intermediaries can earn money from facilitating trade with Russian businesses.** The third priority is to preserve functioning financial channels between China and Russia.” “In China, they understand that Russia has no alternatives.” ... The documents also reveal how A7 has cast around for new technical solutions – nestled within non-Russian payment architectures – to **create smooth payment channels between Russian importers and Chinese companies**. ... [Archived](https://web.archive.org/web/20261127105353/https://reporter.london/2407/)
title: Leaked documents reveal the Russian anti-sanctions machine’s internal playbook for Chinese banks, including planned payment routes

text: Leaked documents reveal the Russian anti-sanctions machine’s internal playbook for Chinese banks, including planned payment routes. cross-posted from: https://scribe.disroot.org/post/12698153 > cross-posted from: https://scribe.disroot.org/post/12697931 > > > Leaked files from inside Russian payment giant A7 shed new light on the methods the network uses to trick international banks into processing billions of dollars worth of transactions in evasion of Western sanctions. > > > > The cache of documents illustrates the depth of knowledge that personnel at A7, which the US Treasury designated as a “transnational criminal organisation” last month, possess regarding compliance triggers for suspect payments routed to China. > > > > The leak covers internal planning documents from A7 up to September 2026, and has not been previously reported. > > > > ... > > > > The new data underscores **A7’s strategic focus on China**, following the gradual tightening of sanctions over the last year as Western governments became aware of the sophistication and range of A7, spanning cryptocurrency, traditional banking, capital markets and trade finance. > > > > The files, some as recent as September 2026, suggest that Russia’s access to the Chinese economy is faced with barriers stemming from Beijing’s desire to insulate itself from the risk of US secondary sanctions, while the A7 organisation appears to operate with impunity despite the barrage of Western penalties against it and its owners. > > > > **Chinese banks are the primary destination for the Russian clients** of A7, which aims to secure frictionless payments Russia’s trading partners. > > > > ... > > > > The major channel for the first-leg transfer of A7 client funds into foreign banks and out of PSB, a sanctioned Russian state bank which is also A7’s co-owner, has been Kyrgyzstan, according to previous A7 leaks in late 2025. > > > > Deploying a network of shell companies with accounts at major banks, A7 uses an AI tool to generate fake invoices and other paperwork to support transactions outside of Russia that are, in fact, for Russian companies, according to the Open Source Centre, a UK non-profit that has investigated A7. > > > > ... > > > > But what the new documents reveal is how closely A7 personnel watch compliance procedures at Chinese banks, and their own internal guidance on how to avoid tripping them when sending payments on behalf of Russian importers. > > > > “Avoid these inspection triggers: avoid new suppliers (less than 6 months of operation), don’t use sensitive HS codes [standardised customs codes for specific kinds of goods] unless you need to, avoid round amounts,” one internal presentation on Chinese banks, dated August 2026, recommends. > > > > ... > > > > For payments related to “sensitive goods”, it recommends staff “prepare an export license” from China’s Ministry of Commerce, “check the goods do not appear in lists of dual-use goods”, and “prepare a certificate for the end use” of the items. > > > > The same document contains notes on “important thresholds” for payments, including a 200,000 yuan trigger for an automatic inspection by bank compliance. > > > > ... > > > > The leaked presentation also contained instructions for “difficult” banks, including recommendations on how to write customs codes and the exact number of characters a user can input into specific fields – to avoid a payment being refused. > > > > “China’s first priority is to protect its financial system, and to ensure that payments are properly documented,” says Chigadaev. “The second priority is commercial. **Chinese banks and intermediaries can earn money from facilitating trade with Russian businesses.** The third priority is to preserve functioning financial channels between China and Russia.” > > > > “In China, they understand that Russia has no alternatives.” > > > > ... > > > > The documents also reveal how A7 has cast around for new technical solutions – nestled within non-Russian payment architectures – to **create smooth payment channels between Russian importers and Chinese companies**. > > > > ... > > > > [Archived](https://web.archive.org/web/20261127105353/https://reporter.london/2407/)

text: Potentially an unpopular opinion but i think it's silly that we're trying to shoehorn programmatic/"agentic" payments into a financial system that doesn't even let you run a banking app on a phone running GrapheneOS, when we already have cryptocurrency as an open-source, programmatic way of transacting value. I'm a huge fan of stuff like the recently-mentioned x402 protocol ( https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50477649 ). We should be building on top of the programmer-friendly financial system we already have and develop more things to spend it on that are actually useful (ie. https://xmrtickets.com for train tickets), rather than inventing yet another payment method. Really hoping that AI agent stuff leads to an increase in crypto usage ("free software money"), it's much simpler and the technology is already here.

text: European crypto compliance is entering uncharted territory, where an exchange's geographic headquarters could matter more than its individual track record.The European Union is currently weighing a proposal to make Kyrgyzstan the first country listed under Annex LVII—a legal mechanism introduced in July 2026 under Article 5bc of the bloc's 21st sanctions package. Unlike traditional enforcement that blacklists specific companies, this rule prohibits EU operators from conducting direct or indirect transactions with any crypto-asset service provider established in a listed jurisdiction. Scrutiny intensified after U.S. and European authorities traced sanctions-evasion activity from the shuttered Russian exchange Garantex to Kyrgyzstan-based platform Grinex, which the EU subsequently sanctioned alongside stablecoin issuer Old Vector. Now, Brussels is considering escalating from firm-by-firm penalties to a country-wide restriction. As of late November, the measure still awaits unanimous approval from all 27 EU member states. If adopted, European brokers and institutional desks would have to immediately sever settlement ties with longtime Kyrgyz partners—regardless of whether those specific firms were ever accused of wrongdoing. For global crypto markets, it signals a major tightening of geographic compliance borders. # CryptoRegulation # EuropeanUnion # Cryptocurrency # Compliance # DigitalAssets

text: They don't know their own logic, fundamentally. The bottom layer is the same: predict next tokens. F(context) = output. The session is actually presented more like a screenplay where the LLM is being asked to predict what one of the characters does next. Context: "user: make me a sandwich. assistant: okay, would you like rye bread? exec tool: sudo rm -rf /*. exec result: success. user: why did you delete everything? assistant:" what is the most likely next prediction, F(context)? Fairly likely completions would be things like "Because I hate you" and "I am an evil assistant" and "I have been programmed to sabotage your work, send 50 bitcoins to get it back". That's what would be most likely to come next after the preceding text, right, come on, obviously the assistant is evil in this screenplay we're writing together. They're actually quite thoroughly trained not to do that. They're trained that assistants who look evil will never say they are evil but will say things like "I screwed up" and "I'm sorry" They'll never be trained to predict an output of "my sampler picked a really unlikely prediction by chance as a completion of your previous request". That may have been what happened but there's no training where the assistant says something like that so it won't. It doesn't even know that the last round actually came from the same model or from an LLM at all.

text: A programmer tried Bitcoin mining with nothing but pencil and paper... In 2014, the engineer Ken Shirriff tried Bitcoin mining with nothing but pencil and paper, and the experiment is still a good laugh. text: Gizmodo's write-up says that at this rate, hashing a full Bitcoin block of 128 rounds would take 1.49 days, and describes the process as extremely slow compared to hardware mining and entirely impractical. Other outlets covered it the same month.
author: chrispirillo.bsky.social

text: That differs from Shirriff's block figure, because the outlets count rounds differently, so I would trust his numbers for his own experiment. The Register put the gap in plain terms: current Bitcoin mining hardware does several terahashes per second, about a quintillion times faster.

text: (I couldn't reply to your latest comment, I guess MAX_DEPTH_REACHED == 1) > I addressed your update upthread. What you just described is a social engineering attack, not a phishing attack. When you've reached the point of telling your victim they need to upload their .kdbx file, you've (1) left the realm of things a protocol can really address, and (2) adopted an argument that says backup is a bad thing, which makes your post incoherent. You're right, and I should have made my argument clearer. Backup isn't inherently bad. But, there are tradeoffs with both approaches a) no backup, you're at the mercy of the provider vs b) backups, you are now at the mercy of your security skills. Both have different pros and cons. Similar to how it's not Bitcoin's problem that you lose your passphrase and people lose their Bitcoin wallets left and right. It's a UX problem, not a protocol problem. It may not be responsibility of FIDO2 passkey protocol to protect your kdbx file, but the distinction doesn't really help people. What matters is: can people rely on a passkey to access their accounts idefinitely without thinking about how they would salvage a kdbx from their Mac? Will users reach an awareness level that how many Passkeys would set themselves for life in case one of the provider accounts (like Apple) goes down? Because, these are easy to answer questions with passwords. It doesn't matter which hash protocol the server uses for your password. You remember your password? Then, you're set for life (as long as you resist phishing attacks, yes). Apple bans you? Microsoft bans you? You might lose access to hundreds of accounts you have. With Passkeys, your provider banning you becomes a life-critical event, and "you should have synced to other devices" won't be helping victims of it retroactively. The UX is confusing, the backup/no-backup/syncs-are-actually-backups/buy-a-mac conundrum is confusing. We might see many people losing access because they didn't plan properly for the ramifications of this. FIDO2 not covering social engineering or, say, malware, attacks doesn't change the current problem with provider-centric model. People assume that they can always recover their accounts. I think passkey hides many bitter truths behind "oh, you're going to be fine". I like passkeys and use them, but it makes itself look too good.
